newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek investment services difficult to monitor.
newsitem.headline: Greek investment services difficult to monitor.

text.p: Greece's capital markets commission lacks adaquate manpower to monitor fully the activities of new investment services firms, the commission's chairman, Stavros Thomadakis, told reporters.

"The capital markets commission has not even a fraction of the Bank of Greece's supervisory capabilites," said Thomadakis. "Our human resources are limited but the new law (regulating investment services firms) will go into effect (on November 1)."
Law 2396/96 was voted by parliament last April and outlines the general framework governing the activities of firms offering investment services in Greece.
He added that the commission was going to beef up its staff to enhance its market monitoring capabilities.

Thomadakis presented three regulations on Thursday concerning the implementation of Law 2396/96. The law embodies the EU directive on investment services and harmonises Greek legislation with that of the European Union.
The first regulation refers to the necessary conditions that firms (EPEYS) with equity capital of "200 million or one billion drachmas" should meet to be given a licence to operate.
The second regulation refers to bookkeeping by EPEYs falling outside the current tax code.

"The main goal of the requested figures is the ability of the investor and the supervisory authority to look into the transactions of the firm (EPEY) and confirm that investors' orders have been executed."

The third regulation refers to Greek depository receipts (ELPIS) and sets the criteria for granting a licence to credit institutions that issue ELPIS. ELPIS is the Greek version of U.S ADRs. --Dimitris Kontogiannis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
